cards.front: Why is var f = () -> "hi"; a compile error?
cards.back: A lambda has no type on its own — with var the initializer is typed standalone, with no assignment context to target
cards.extra: JLS 14.4.1 types the initializer "as if it did not appear in an assignment context", so a lambda or method reference leaves nothing to infer. javac: cannot infer type for local variable f (lambda expression needs an explicit target-type). Declare the functional interface instead: Supplier<String> f = () -> "hi";.
cards.example:
var f = () -> "hi";          // error: lambda expression needs an explicit target-type
Supplier<String> g = () -> "hi";   // ok

cards.front: Why is var a = {1, 2}; a compile error?
cards.back: An array initializer carries no type of its own — it is legal only inside an array declaration or an array creation expression
cards.extra: JLS 14.4 lists var f = { 6 }; among the illegal forms, and javac reports array initializer needs an explicit target-type. Write the array creation explicitly: var a = new int[]{1, 2};.
cards.example:
var a = {1, 2};              // error: array initializer needs an explicit target-type
var b = new int[]{1, 2};       // ok, b is int[]

cards.back: ArrayList<Object> — the diamond has no target type, so nothing constrains the element type
cards.extra: With var the constructor argument is Object, and adding a String does not narrow it: javac still rejects ArrayList<String> s = list; with incompatible types: ArrayList<Object> cannot be converted to ArrayList<String>. Put the argument on the right — new ArrayList<String>() — when the element type matters.
cards.example:
var list = new ArrayList<>();
list.add("x");
ArrayList<String> s = list;   // error: ArrayList<Object> is not ArrayList<String>
